newsitem.title: POLAND: FEATURE - Election hopes of Polish right focus on Solidarity.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Election hopes of Polish right focus on Solidarity.

text.p: A strong new right-wing alliance has formed around Poland's Solidarity trade union to fight this year's parliamentary election, proclaiming Catholic, patriotic values and deep hostility to the ruling ex-communists.
Solidarity Election Action (AWS) groups more than 30 of Poland's fractious little opposition parties that the union, which toppled communism in 1989, managed to unite last year.
This gives hope to a right so split that it was beaten by ex-communists in 1993 elections and saw their chief Aleksander Kwasniewski win Poland's presidency from Lech Walesa in 1995.
Opinion polls suggest the AWS, if it stays together, could come top of the polls due in September or October.
EXACT PROGRAMME TO BE READIED JUST BEFORE THE POLLS
What exactly this would mean for Poland and its economy is not yet fully apparent, as AWS is still working on its programme and there are significant differences between its parties.
Solidarity union president Marian Krzaklewski told Reuters it will reveal its detailed programme, as ready-drafted laws, just six weeks or a month before the vote.

The union is dominant in the AWS and while it does not seek government posts for itself, it will sign contracts with politicians to ensure they do not abandon the agreed AWS programme once they have used the alliance to gain power.

Krzaklewski, a dark-haired engineer whose triumphant smile and strong jaw leads hostile cartoonists to depict him as Italian dictator Benito Mussolini, said he would remain union chief, at least until 1998, rather than be prime minister.

"If I left my post there would be a leadership struggle which could disrupt the union, which in the first phase will be the guarantor of the programme contracts and cannot be destabilised," he said in an interview.

Solidarity's arch-enemy is the Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) of former communists, which has ruled along with the Peasant Party since 1993, while pursuing some market reforms and seeking fast membership of the European Union and NATO.
Solidarity wants a new Polish constitution based on religious ideas, rather than a secular one being shaped by the left, and it aims to revert to a tough anti-abortion law.
It wants to investigate officials for past cooperation with communist security police and to sweep former communist appointees from the many posts they hold in state-controlled firms.

Opponents of the AWS and of its smaller right-wing rival the Movement for the Reconstruction of Poland (ROP), accuse both of economic populism which might deter foreign investment and delay Poland's entry into the European Union.

Some say its aim of settling scores from the communist past will polarise society, while Solidarity's dominance in the AWS could mean a country unduly influenced by a two-million-strong union into policies such as pouring cash into dying industries.
SOLIDARITY PROMISES MORE MARKET-ORIENTED ECONOMY
Krzaklewski said foreign investors would gain from an AWS victory.
"An AWS win would mean a more market-oriented economy, stripped of left-overs and patronage from the old system, decentralised, less political, more privatised," he said.

Solidarity's central economic idea is privatisation of remaining state enterprises and other assets such as land and buildings by issuing coupons to the people, going much further than the current policy of selling of firms piecemeal and a limited mass privatisation scheme involving just 500 firms.
This privatisation would yield capital for a vital reform setting up pension, benefits and health insurance funds to replace the present costly, inefficient social security system.

Krzaklewski said half of these privatised assets would go to the people as coupons, while half would provide capital for funds -- including a restructuring fund which would get 10-15 percent and would help improve firms in the coupon scheme.
"We would like to allocate 10 percent of banks to the health care and education sectors, to give them a one-off financial impulse," he said.
AWS also stresses the fast return to former owners of assets, especially land, which had been taken over by the communists.
Krzaklewski savaged the current mass privatisation scheme and said AWS would investigate some past sell-offs that might have been shady, but he acknowledged there was little scope to undo them.
"The right of property is sacred, and we understand that some processes cannot be reversed," Krzaklewski said.

He said the AWS would, however, try to delay until after the election the impending privatisation of major firms including giants of the telecommunications, copper and fuels sectors, so the proceeds could be used according to its own plans.
CAUTION OVER PRICE OF EU MEMBERSHIP
He accused the left, which wants Poland in the European Union by 2000 and in monetary union soon after, of playing down dangers of job losses in areas like steel and farming.

"Decisions are made by a few people in offices, while society is told that the EU means a good uncle arriving with cases of cash and everyone will get higher pay and living standards. That is not how it is," Krzaklewski said.
He said the AWS favoured a Europe of Motherlands concept, involving minimum interference in Poland's laws and affairs.
Asked whether the AWS thought Poland should join monetary union, he said it would decide a policy by June.
The AWS would seek longer adjustment periods in talks with the EU for Polish sectors such as shipbuilding, steel and farms, and was against letting foreigners buy Polish land.

Krzaklewski is unabashed about aiming to spend on loss-making industries including shipyards and coal mining, saying it is better to invest in restructuring them, while retraining any laid-off workers, rather pay out dole.

He says the AWS wants workers to sign long-term collective labour agreements, at local or enterprise levels, and expects unions to be formally consulted by government on some issues such as setting minimum wage levels.
"This is not interference in the legislative or executive authorities, but very useful consultation," he said.
